sections.h2: What does a New Mexico quitclaim deed actually do?
sections.html:
A New Mexico quitclaim deed passes whatever interest the signer holds in a piece of real estate, and the statutory form promises nothing beyond that. Section 47-1-44 NMSA 1978 prints the short forms used for conveyances in the state. The warranty deed form ends with the words "with warranty covenants." The quitclaim form has no such line.

The quitclaim form reads, in outline: for consideration paid, the grantor quitclaims to the grantee, whose address is stated, the described real estate in a named county in New Mexico. A legal description follows, then the witness and seal line, then a place to add the acknowledgment. You can read the forms in the statute text on Justia.

That gap in wording matters when a house is being sold. A seller who signs a quitclaim is not promising that the title is clean, that nobody else owns a share, or that old liens were paid. The buyer receives the seller's interest and carries the risk of everything else. Quitclaim deeds therefore show up most often between relatives, after a divorce, when a name is added or removed, and when a boundary or a gap in the record needs to be cleaned up.

The Santa Fe County Clerk makes a related point from the recording desk. Its office says it is not bonded to tell anyone whether a warranty deed, a special warranty deed or a quitclaim deed is the right form, and it suggests asking a real estate attorney.

sections.h2: How is a quitclaim deed recorded in New Mexico, and what does it cost?
sections.html:
The signed deed goes to the county clerk of the county where the property sits, and the statutory recording fee is $25 per document. Section 14-8-15 NMSA 1978 says a clerk may not accept an instrument for filing until the fees are paid. It also adds $25 for each extra block of ten or fewer entries to the county recording index once a document has more than ten entries. Of each $25 fee, $18 goes to the county general fund and $7 to the clerk's recording and filing fund.

Counties set their own handling rules on top of that. The table below pulls together what the statute and the Santa Fe County Clerk's recording page say.

ItemWhat the source saysSource
Base recording fee$25 for each document filed or recorded14-8-15 NMSA 1978
Large documentsAnother $25 for each added block of ten or fewer index entries beyond the first ten14-8-15 NMSA 1978
SignaturesSanta Fe County asks for the original signature and the notary's original signatureSanta Fe County Clerk
Notary blockMust be on the document, with a legible seal that does not sit over signatures or printed textSanta Fe County Clerk
Electronic filingAvailable through Simplifile or CSC, which charge a convenience fee on top of recording feesSanta Fe County Clerk

Other counties may run things differently, so call the clerk in the county where the house is. The Santa Fe County recording page is a good model of what to expect.

sections.h2: Who has to sign a quitclaim deed on a married couple's house?
sections.html:
Both spouses must sign in most cases. Section 40-3-13 NMSA 1978 says spouses must join in transfers of community real property, and in transfers of separate real property that they own together as joint tenants or tenants in common. A transfer attempted by one spouse alone in violation of that rule is void, with one exception: either spouse may transfer directly to the other without the other joining.

The statute leaves two doors open. A spouse can sign alone under a validly executed and recorded power of attorney, and a spouse who did not join can later ratify the instrument in writing. Separate property owned by only one spouse can generally be transferred without the other's joinder.

For a seller the practical lesson is simple. If you are married and the house was bought during the marriage, plan on both signatures.

sections.h2: What happens if a quitclaim deed is never recorded?
sections.html:
An unrecorded deed still binds the two people who signed it, but it can lose to a later buyer who did not know about it. Section 14-9-3 NMSA 1978 says an unrecorded deed does not affect the title or rights of a purchaser, a good faith mortgagee or a judgment lien creditor who had no knowledge of the unrecorded instrument.

The annotations spell out the consequences:

  • A deed that is not recorded is good between grantor and grantee, and it divests the grantor's title as between them.
  • In one quiet title case, a buyer who purchased in good faith, for value and without knowledge of an earlier unrecorded deed won, even though the buyer's own paper was a quitclaim.

If you received a house by quitclaim from a parent or former partner, record it before you do anything else. A sale cannot close cleanly while the last deed in the chain sits in a drawer.

sections.h2: Does a quitclaim deed need an affidavit filed with the county assessor?
sections.html:
For residential property, usually yes. Section 7-38-12.1 NMSA 1978 requires the person presenting a deed for recording on residential property to also file an affidavit with the county assessor within thirty days of the date of filing with the county clerk. Either the transferor, the transferee or their authorized agents may sign it.

The affidavit is limited to the names and mailing addresses of all transferors and transferees, the legal description, the full consideration paid or exchanged along with the terms of the sale and any seller incentives, and the value and description of personal property included in the price. The assessor keeps the original as a confidential record, and the affidavit is not part of the valuation record.

The statute lists many deeds that do not need the affidavit. Among them:

  • A quitclaim deed to quiet title or clear boundary disputes.
  • An instrument between husband and wife, or parent and child, with only nominal actual consideration.
  • An instrument that confirms or corrects a deed already recorded.
  • A deed from a sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • An instrument delivered to establish a gift or a distribution from an estate or trust.

The Santa Fe County Clerk adds a related duty. The clerk sends the assessor a copy of every recorded document, but the person receiving the property is responsible for notifying the assessor so the right person gets the tax bill. Unpaid property tax can eventually lead to a tax sale.

sections.h2: How do tax sale deeds compare with quitclaim deeds?
sections.html:
The New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department says the deed it issues after a delinquent tax auction is equivalent to a quitclaim deed. The deed conveys all of the former owner's interest as of the date the state's lien for real property taxes arose, subject only to perfected interests that existed before that date. The department also states that New Mexico warrants no title to property sold at its auctions.

The department explains that an interest is perfected when the deed or lien is recorded with the county clerk where the property is located. Its guidance adds that the tax deed can be used as the basis to begin clearing title through the court.

Annotations to the Property Tax Code add that grantees under a quitclaim deed from a tax sale purchaser take subject to defects they knew about, or that the record would have shown. The department's delinquent property tax auction page sets out the terms.

sections.h2: When does a quitclaim deed work for selling a New Mexico house, and when does it fall short?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed works when everyone involved understands that only the signer's actual interest is changing hands. It falls short when a buyer expects promises the form does not contain.

It usually works for:

  • Moving a house between family members who know the history of the property.
  • Removing a former spouse or co-owner who agrees to give up their share.
  • Passing along an inherited house where the heirs have settled who owns what, and the paperwork needs to catch up.

It usually falls short when:

  • The seller wants the buyer to rely on a promise that the title is free of claims.
  • Co-owners or a spouse have not signed, so part of the interest never moved.
  • Liens, unpaid property tax or an old mortgage remain on record.
  • The house is occupied by someone with a claim, such as a tenant or relative, that the deed does not address.

A quitclaim can move an interest quickly, but it cannot make a lien, a missing co-owner or a tax debt disappear. Those items stay with the property, and a buyer's title review will find them. Cash Home Buyers does not promise a price in advance, and each New Mexico house gets looked at on its own facts.

faqs.q: Is a New Mexico quitclaim deed the same as a warranty deed?
faqs.a: No. The statutory warranty deed form in 47-1-44 NMSA 1978 ends with warranty covenants, and the quitclaim form carries none. A quitclaim transfers only the interest the signer holds.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in New Mexico?
faqs.a: The statutory fee is $25 per document under 14-8-15 NMSA 1978. An extra $25 applies for each additional block of ten or fewer index entries beyond the first ten. E-recording vendors add their own convenience fee.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed have to be notarized?
faqs.a: For recording, yes in practice. The Santa Fe County Clerk will not accept a document without a proper notary block. Case annotations under 14-9-3 note that an acknowledgment is not essential to a deed's validity between the parties, but an unrecorded deed can lose to a later good faith buyer.

faqs.q: Can one spouse sign a quitclaim deed alone in New Mexico?
faqs.a: Generally no for community real property. Section 40-3-13 says a transfer by one spouse alone is void, except a direct transfer to the other spouse. A recorded power of attorney or a later written ratification can change the result.

faqs.q: Do I file anything with the county assessor after recording a quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Often yes for residential property. An affidavit is due to the assessor within thirty days of filing with the clerk under 7-38-12.1, unless an exemption applies, such as a quitclaim to quiet title or a transfer between parent and child for nominal consideration.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house I received by quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Yes, you can sell whatever interest you hold. The buyer and the title company will review the chain of title, and anything the deed did not clear, such as liens or an unsigned co-owner, will surface at that point.
